t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: What Confidential Computing Is: Trust the Silicon
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: What Confidential Computing Is: Trust the Silicon
description: Confidential computing protects data in use: Intel SGX carves enclaves — encrypted memory regions even the OS and hypervisor cannot read — while AMD SEV encrypts entire VMs (SEV-SNP adding integrity and attestation). Remote attestation lets a client verify the enclave's identity and code measurement before sending secrets. The threat model is the untrusted host: the cloud operator, the compromised hypervisor — excluded by hardware.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Intel SGX: Enclaves in the Process
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Intel SGX: Enclaves in the Process
description: SGX enclaves live inside the process address space: ECALLs enter, OCALLs exit, and the Enclave Page Cache (EPC, ~128MB-1GB depending on platform) holds the encrypted pages. The programming model is partition — secrets and their computation inside, everything else outside — with SDKs (Intel SGX SDK) and frameworks (Gramine, Occlum) easing the port. The art is minimizing the enclave boundary: small TCB, small attack surface.
key_facts: Encrypted pages even the OS cannot read

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: AMD SEV: Encrypted Virtual Machines
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: AMD SEV: Encrypted Virtual Machines
description: SEV encrypts VM memory with per-VM keys the hypervisor never sees; SEV-SNP adds integrity protection and a richer attestation report (the chip signs the VM's measurement plus the platform state). The model is lift-and-shift: whole VMs become confidential with minimal code changes — the operational opposite of SGX's partitioning. For defense clouds, SEV-SNP is how tenant workloads stay secret from the provider.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Remote Attestation: Prove Before Trust
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Remote Attestation: Prove Before Trust
description: Attestation is the protocol: the hardware signs a quote containing the enclave/VM measurement; the verifier checks the signature chain to the manufacturer's root and compares the measurement against policy. Only then do secrets flow (keys provisioned to the attested enclave). The PKI (Intel's IAS/DCAP, AMD's KDS) is the trust root — understand it, monitor it, plan for its rotation.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Your First Enclave: Hello, Sealed World
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Your First Enclave: Hello, Sealed World
description: The hello-world: write the enclave that seals a secret (encrypt with the enclave's sealing key, bound to the measurement), unseal it on the next run, and print the attestation quote. The sealing key never leaves the hardware; the secret never leaves the enclave unencrypted. From here: the secret is a model weight, a private key, a database key — the pattern generalizes to anything that must stay secret from the host.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Partitioning: What Goes Inside
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Partitioning: What Goes Inside
description: The SGX design question is the boundary: put the crypto and the key handling inside; keep the UI, the network, the parsing outside. Every ECALL is a potential confused-deputy; every OCALL leaks a bit of control flow. The discipline is data-flow review: what crosses the boundary, in which direction, and what it reveals. Small enclaves are auditable enclaves.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Frameworks: Gramine and Occlum
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Frameworks: Gramine and Occlum
description: Porting to SGX is eased by library OS frameworks: Gramine and Occlum run unmodified applications inside enclaves, handling the ECALL/OCALL boundary and shielding system calls. The trade is TCB size — the LibOS is inside the trust boundary — versus porting effort. For lift-and-shift confidential computing, frameworks are the practical path; for minimal TCB, the SDK's partitioning. Choose by threat model, not convenience.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Side Channels: The Enclave's Adversary
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Side Channels: The Enclave's Adversary
description: Enclaves face side channels: page-fault controlled channels, cache timing, speculative execution variants. The defenses are constant-time code, ORAM-like access patterns where needed, and the platform's microcode mitigations — plus the honest assessment that some adversaries (the malicious OS with full observation) are partially in scope. The threat model must name the side-channel assumptions explicitly.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Defensive Uses: The Secret-Keeping Cloud
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Defensive Uses: The Secret-Keeping Cloud
description: Confidential computing's defensive value is computing on secrets without trusting the computer: model weights that stay secret from the cloud operator, key-management services the provider cannot read, multi-party analytics on combined datasets no party reveals. Attestation makes it verifiable — the client proves the enclave before trusting it with the secret. This is the architecture for 'use the cloud, trust the silicon'.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Key Management in Enclaves
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Key Management in Enclaves
description: The killer app is key management: master keys that exist only inside enclaves, released to attested workloads, never visible to operators. The enclave becomes the HSM-as-software — with attestation as the access policy. The operational discipline is the attestation policy's maintenance: acceptable measurements updated with each release, revocation when a measurement is compromised.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Debugging: The Opaque Box
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Debugging: The Opaque Box
description: Enclave debugging is constrained by design: debug enclaves (unsigned, debuggable) for development, production enclaves opaque. The tools are enclave-aware debuggers and the disciplined use of OCALL logging — never log secrets. The classic bug is the boundary: wrong ECALL parameters, uninitialized outside memory. Debug the boundary first.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Performance: The Enclave Tax
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Performance: The Enclave Tax
description: Enclaves cost: ECALL transitions (~microseconds), EPC paging when overcommitted (the cliff — avoid it), memory encryption overhead (single digits percent). SEV's cost is lower (near-native for many workloads). The engineering is budgeting: keep the working set in EPC, minimize crossings, measure on the target SKU. The tax is real but payable — and the security is worth more than the cycles.

t: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Testing: Attestation in CI
title: Intel SGX / AMD SEV: Testing: Attestation in CI
description: Confidential workloads are tested with attestation mocked in dev and real in staging: the CI runs the enclave logic in simulation, the staging environment runs the attestation ceremony against real hardware. The policy (acceptable measurements) is tested too — a release that changes the measurement must update the policy, and the CI verifies the pair. Untested attestation is untrusted attestation.
